paragraph.text: E13. "He eats meat, but he's a good person"

veganism criticizes an act, not the character of the people who do it. Generous, honest and loving people also take part in unjust practices when those practices are normal in their time. Saying someone is good doesn't answer the question of what happens to the animal, and that person's goodness is precisely what makes it likely they'll change once they see the problem.
"My dad eats meat and he's the most honest person I know. Are you saying he's evil?"
A good person, in general, doesn't routinely do seriously wrong things.
Many people who are recognizably good eat meat every day.
So eating meat can't be seriously wrong.
And whoever says it is, is accusing people of wickedness they don't deserve.

P2 is true, and it's important to say so plainly. The problem lies in P1, which confuses having good character with getting everything right, and in C2, which confuses criticizing a practice with condemning people.
: P1 is refuted by the whole of moral history, in which good people took part in injustices that custom accepted.
"I know great people who eat meat."
"My grandma eats meat and she's the kindest person in the world."
"Vegans think they're better than everyone." (which leads to L1)
"A morality that condemns almost every virtuous agent is probably mistaken."
"I'm a good person, I give to charity, I help others."

A person can be really good and still do something that hurts someone without realizing it. Sometimes nobody explained it to them, or everyone around them does the same. That doesn't mean they're bad. It means they can learn. And since they're a good person, when they understand that the little pig suffers, they'll very likely want to stop.

No one is saying he's evil. Good people also take part in wrong things when those things are normal and no one questions them. The question isn't about his character; it's about what happens to the animal. And it's precisely because he's a good person that he'd probably care, if he looked at it.
"If he's a good person, do you think he'd agree with what happens to the animals if he saw it up close?"
The argument swaps one question for another:
Someone's character, across their whole life
The two are independent. A kind person can do an act that causes harm, and an unpleasant person can do a right act. Veganism asks a question of the second kind.

text.bold: 1. Good character doesn't guarantee right acts.

paragraph.text: Moral history is full of kind, honest, charitable people who took part in practices now seen as unjust, because they were normal and no one around them questioned them. That didn't make them monsters; it made the practice invisible to them.

text.bold: 2. The criticism is of the practice, not the person.

paragraph.text: Saying an act is wrong isn't saying the person who does it is bad. One can act wrongly out of ignorance, habit, or because the environment makes the act automatic. Philosophy has long distinguished assessing the act from assessing the agent.

text.bold: 3. The animal isn't affected by the eater's character.

paragraph.text: For the pig in the slaughterhouse, it makes no difference whether the final consumer is generous or selfish. The harm is the same.

text.bold: 4. The person's goodness is a reason for hope, not a defense.

paragraph.text: If they care about others, they'll probably care about animals too once they see what happens. Many good people have changed for exactly that reason.

text.bold: 5. The argument often appears as a preemptive defense.

paragraph.text: Research on so-called do-gooder derogation shows that people tend to feel judged by those who follow a different moral position, even when no one has accused them. "Are you calling me evil?" often answers an accusation that wasn't made.
Meat eaters tend to expect moral judgment from vegetarians, and this increases their rejection of them
The halo effect: the overall impression of someone colors the assessment of specific traits and acts
"Normal" is one of the four most common justifications for eating meat
(d) The strongest counter-reply: a morality that condemns almost everyone is suspect

The most serious version says: if a moral theory concludes that almost everyone, including the most admirable people, does something seriously wrong every day, that's evidence against the theory. Our judgments about who is good would be more reliable than an abstract argument.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: That test would have failed before.

paragraph.text: In various eras, almost the whole of society, including its most respected members, accepted practices we now recognize as unjust. If the rule were "what good people do can't be serious", none of those practices would have been corrected.
It starts from facts almost everyone accepts: animals feel pain and fear, and causing unnecessary suffering is wrong. The conclusion comes from common judgments, not against them.

text.bold: Condemning the act isn't condemning the agent.

paragraph.text: The theory doesn't need to say these people are bad; it only needs to say they're mistaken about a practice, which is compatible with their being admirable.
L1 "Vegans are annoying and think they are better"
The feeling of being judged becomes a defense of character
If everyone does it, including good people, it can't be wrong
The good person also says they love animals
E10 "Nobody's perfect; I do what I can"
General goodness becomes a license not to change
Custom explains why good people don't see the problem
Swaps "does the act harm someone?" for "is the person good?"
Attributes to veganism the accusation that meat eaters are evil
Uses a good overall impression to judge a specific act
Takes the virtue of the doer as proof that the deed is right

text.bold: Recognizes that good people err on other subjects.

paragraph.text: The same person admits that someone they love can have prejudices or habits that harm others.

text.bold: Assesses acts without looking at character when they're the victim.

paragraph.text: If a pleasant person harms us, the harm is still harm.

text.bold: Admires people who changed a habit for moral reasons.

paragraph.text: And that presupposes the old habit was a mistake, even in someone good.
The person's general goodness extends to what they eat
Feeling judged triggers a defensive reaction against someone who didn't even accuse
"It's normal" works as proof that nothing is wrong
The principle being tested is: "if good people routinely do something, it can't be wrong".
They'd be acceptable as long as respected people took part in them
Jokes or exclusions by pleasant people wouldn't be a problem
Drink-driving would be acceptable if the driver were a good person
The risk to others doesn't change

It gets something important right: people who eat meat aren't bad for doing so, and treating people as villains is unfair and counterproductive. Most people grew up in a culture where eating animals is so normal the question never came up. Defending animals calls for firmness about the practice and generosity toward people.
But someone's goodness doesn't change what happens to the animal. And it's exactly because so many people are good that the question is worth asking.
